keyVerseText: And when they were come to the multitude, there came to him a certain man, kneeling down to him, and saying,
rootMeaning: The word γονυπετέω (gonypetéō) is a compound derived from γόνυ (góny), meaning 'knee,' and an alternate form of the verb πίπτω (to fall). Its literal sense is to 'fall on the knee,' emphasizing a physical act of bending or bowing at the knee. This etymology highlights a posture of submission or reverence that goes beyond the simple act of kneeling, conveying a deliberate lowering of oneself in humility or respect.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, γονυπετέω appears four times and consistently conveys the physical act of kneeling or bowing the knee. The top translations include 'kneeling down' (twice), 'they bowed the knee' (once), and 'kneeled' (once), indicating a close semantic range focused on reverent bodily posture. This consistency suggests the word is used to describe acts of worship, supplication, or humble approach toward God or others, underscoring the importance of physical expression in spiritual encounters.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the concept of γονυπετέω enriches our understanding of worship and prayer as involving the whole person—body and spirit. To bow the knee is to acknowledge God's authority and our dependence on Him, embodying humility and submission before the Almighty. This posture reflects the heart attitude believers are called to have, recognizing God's sovereignty and grace. Christ himself, as the perfect example, invites us into this posture of reverence, teaching that true faith expresses itself in both inward devotion and outward acts of surrender.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 17:14 describes a man approaching Jesus 'kneeling down to him,' using γονυπετέω to capture the depth of his humility and earnestness. This physical act of falling on the knee conveys the man's desperate plea and recognition of Jesus' power and authority. The word enriches the scene by highlighting not just the man's words but his reverent posture, inviting readers to see faith as involving heartfelt submission and trust in Christ's ability to heal and save.
